extracted.intended_audience: scientific peer reviewers (graduate students, postdocs, researchers) reviewing manuscripts for F1000Research and similar journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing clear, constructive, and useful peer review reports of scientific manuscripts (public peer reviews on F1000Research), including organization, tone, statistical critique, and section-specific advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay In Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep comments within the scope of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from Sheila McCormick: focus on issues directly relevant to the manuscript rather than extraneous topics or broad agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Be constructive; view your reviewer role as an opportunity to help improve the paper you are reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from Bruce MacIver and illustrated by example reviews that explain why results are important, point out specific issues, and offer concrete suggestions for revision rather than only listing faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage Your Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t underestimate the time it takes to carefully analyze a manuscript and write a constructive review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from Hugues Abriel: plan sufficient time to read and think about the paper thoroughly before writing the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize Your Comments: Major vs Minor
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing your specific concerns, separate them into 'major' and 'minor' points; if your list is very long, consolidate the most minor points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from Robert Fisher and illustrated by organized example reviews: put highest-priority, decision-influencing items (major) first; group minor editorial/formatting/clarity issues together to avoid burying main concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus On The Science (tolerance for non-native English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on scientific content; if the paper is in English but not written by a native speaker, be tolerant and only point out issues that change the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sue Malcolm's guidance: do not penalize non-native phrasing unless it affects interpretation; correct only wording that alters the science or conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start At The End (assess conclusion first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the conclusion paragraph first to assess how exciting and consequential the science is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vincent Rotello: a good conclusion tells you how the paper will change the field; use it to quickly judge the paper's central claim and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider The Statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on the number of replicates, controls, and the statistical analyses used to assess robustness of the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christine Mummery: check sample sizes, experimental controls and whether appropriate statistical tests were applied. Example critique shows how circular analysis can inflate apparent accuracy and why authors should provide clarification or code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request Appropriate Statistical Methods / Reanalysis When Needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify incorrect or inappropriate statistical procedures and recommend alternatives or reanalysis where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include noting violated assumptions (e.g., ANCOVA with non‑common slopes), not retaining nonsignificant interaction terms, treating species as fixed vs random factors, recommending mixed models, Johnson–Neyman method, inclusion of phylogeny where relevant, and asking for reanalysis using correct methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Methods Reporting and Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure methods are described with sufficient detail for replication and clarity (measurement protocols, variable definitions, categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: clarify whether auditory and visual distances were measured the same way; state whether litter cover was recorded as continuous percentage or categorical and define categories; ask for analysis scripts when analysis procedures are unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Figures, Tables and Results Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that figures/tables present appropriate statistics, are internally consistent with text, and have clear captions (include equations or model summaries where useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: request post-hoc test results (e.g., Tukey HSD) when means/SDs are shown; reconcile apparent inconsistencies between text claims and reported R-squared values; suggest placing linear equation in figure caption; ask that statistics for figure panels be presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Correlation from Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag causal language not supported by the data and recommend rephrasing to reflect correlation where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: point out where conclusions assert causality ('That is because…') when only correlational data are presented and suggest more cautious wording or further analyses to support causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight Important or Novel Results and Their Implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the most important findings and suggest ways to better emphasize or explore their implications in Discussion/Conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: indicate if a result (e.g., pruning effect) warrants more discussion, whether it could suggest management prescriptions, and recommend linking to related literature or societal/management implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Positive and Explicit About Strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is good, explicitly say so and describe what is strong about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthony Imbalzano and example reviews: praise conceptual advances, clarity, or novel findings and suggest further useful experiments; positive feedback is encouraged and valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Public Peer Review Examples and Other Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from publicly available peer review reports and external guides to inform tone, level of detail, and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000Research points reviewers to selected peer review reports, 'Peer Review: The Nuts And Bolts' (Sense About Science), and 'A Guide to Peer Review in Ecology and Evolution' (British Ecological Society) as exemplars and further reading.
